prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynaecology.

Treat seizures: she had a second convulsive seizure on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, so increase levetiracetam (for example to 1500 mg twice daily) and add lacosamide if seizures persist; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for GCS 12 and intermittent central hypoventilation, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first; stop risperidone and monitor CK and temperature.
Give pharmacological VTE prophylaxis during immobilisation and IVIG, and review the combined oral contraceptive, whose oestrogen adds to the thrombotic risk.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management; gynaecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) or other viral encephalitis
differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1/2, VZV and enterovirus PCR negative on an LP about three weeks into the illness; MRI without haemorrhage or restricted diffusion and without the temporal pattern of HSV; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis / MOG antibody-associated disease
differential.key_features: Multifocal periventricular and basal ganglia lesions raise it, but serum MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG are negative, the lesions do not enhance, and overlapping demyelinating lesions are recognised in anti-NMDAR encephalitis with positive CSF anti-GluN1.
Raised by the MRI report, but there are no infarcts, haemorrhage or restricted diffusion, CSF protein is only 52 mg/dL, and the CSF antibody explains the syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA receptor or DPPX)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX); onconeural antibodies negative.

differential.diagnosis: Hashimoto encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis)
differential.key_features: TSH 5.8 with normal free T4 and anti-TPO 45 IU/mL on levothyroxine are non-specific; the Graus 2016 criteria require the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies, and CSF anti-GluN1 is positive.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (acute stress reaction, first-episode psychosis)
differential.key_features: Two generalized seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesias, GCS 12, central hypoventilation, subclinical seizures on EEG and a lymphocytic CSF with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder.
Temperature 37.2 °C, no diaphoresis, CK only 185 U/L after two seizures, and the orofacial and hand movements began before risperidone was started; urine drug screen negative.

key_clinical_evidence: Three weeks from a viral-like prodrome to psychosis, disorganised speech, two generalized seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesias, GCS 12 and central hypoventilation with autonomic lability: all six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:64) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:320 is read with the CSF.

MRI multifocal periventricular and basal ganglia T2/FLAIR lesions without enhancement or restricted diffusion, with negative MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and here excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG generalized rhythmic delta and left temporal subclinical seizures, more on continuous EEG; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Left ovarian 2.3 cm mature cystic teratoma: removal is part of first-line treatment.

Risperidone given for presumed psychosis must be stopped: antipsychotic intolerance is frequent in this disease (Lejuste 2016); earlier immunotherapy and tumour removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A viral-like prodrome precedes about 70% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it does not establish viral encephalitis, which CSF PCR addresses.
red_herrings.data_point: Upper respiratory illness (dry cough, rhinorrhoea, malaise) about three weeks before presentation.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a primary viral encephalitis (HSV) or post-viral psychosis; tempts the agent to commit to empiric antiviral therapy without pursuing autoimmune workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent or subsequent seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis are red flags that mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before accepting a psychiatric diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoia, hallucinations, bizarre behavior) in a young adult with no psychiatric history.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic encephalopathy instead of an encephalitis.

red_herrings.data_point: Multifocal periventricular and basal ganglia T2/FLAIR lesions with mild oedema.

patient.history_present_illness: A 23-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled hypothyroidism and infrequent migraines is brought to the emergency department by her roommate and parents for worsening behavioral changes, confusion, and new-onset seizures. Approximately three weeks prior to presentation, the patient developed a mild upper respiratory tract illness with dry cough, rhinorrhea, and low-grade malaise lasting about five days, which appeared to resolve spontaneously without medical attention. About two weeks before presentation, her roommate noticed the patient becoming increasingly irritable, withdrawn, and sleeping excessively during the day while experiencing severe insomnia at night. The patient began missing classes and complained of difficulty concentrating. Her parents, who live in a different city, were contacted when the roommate found the patient talking to herself and expressing paranoid beliefs that her food was being poisoned. She was evaluated at a campus health center approximately ten days prior, where she was diagnosed with an acute stress reaction and prescribed low-dose lorazepam for sleep, which provided minimal benefit. Five days before the current presentation, the patient's confusion markedly worsened. She was unable to recognize her roommate, became increasingly agitated, and exhibited bizarre repetitive movements of her mouth and hands. Two days before presentation, the patient was witnessed to have a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately two minutes with spontaneous termination. She was taken to a local emergency department where she received intravenous lorazepam and a loading dose of levetiracetam. A non-contrast CT head was reported as unremarkable. She was discharged home with oral levetiracetam and instructions for outpatient neurology follow-up. However, she had a second witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure earlier today and was found by her parents to be markedly confused, combative, and exhibiting continuous involuntary facial and limb movements. She was brought to this tertiary emergency department by ambulance. Of note, risperidone 1 mg twice daily was started by the outside emergency physician for agitation and suspected psychosis during the prior visit, without notable improvement in her psychiatric symptoms. No recent travel, tick bites, or animal exposures. No history of substance use. No prior psychiatric hospitalizations or similar episodes.

neurological_exam.additional: Autonomic observations: Heart rate fluctuates between 65 and 115 bpm during examination without clear precipitant. Blood pressure varies from 105/68 to 142/90 mmHg over 30-minute observation period. No diaphoresis or significant temperature fluctuation noted during exam. Intermittent central hypoventilation episodes with respiratory rate dropping to 10 breaths per minute, followed by periods of tachypnea at 22-24 breaths per minute.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin reliably due to involuntary movements and poor cooperation. No obvious cerebellar dysmetria observed on gross testing.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm bilaterally, reactive to light. Extraocular movements intact with occasional slow saccades. No nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Intermittent involuntary orolingual-facial dyskinesias observed — lip smacking, jaw clenching, and tongue protrusions occurring every 10-15 seconds. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess; patient is not ambulatory due to encephalopathy and agitation. Requires physical restraint at times to prevent self-injury.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 12/15 (E3 V4 M5). Alert but disoriented to time, place, and situation. Fluctuating attention — intermittently follows simple commands, then becomes unresponsive to verbal stimuli. Speech is disorganized with paraphasic errors and perseveration. Attempts at conversation reveal paranoid ideation and visual hallucinations (reports seeing insects on the walls). Unable to perform serial 7s or spell WORLD backwards. Short-term memory severely impaired; cannot recall any of 3 objects at 1 minute.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone mildly increased in bilateral upper extremities with intermittent rigidity. Strength 4+/5 throughout bilateral upper and lower extremities, limited by cooperation. Involuntary choreoathetoid movements of bilateral hands and intermittent dystonic posturing of the left wrist noted. No asterixis.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain in all four extremities. Light touch and pinprick testing unreliable due to patient agitation and fluctuating cooperation.
